reframing_when: The question asks about a solution or product feature when the real question is about the outcome the user is trying to achieve — the drill is being discussed instead of the hole.
The question confuses the means (a specific tool, process, or approach) with the end (the progress the person is trying to make) — solution-space is being explored before problem-space is defined.
The question assumes the current framing of the problem is correct without checking whether the customer, stakeholder, or user would describe their need the same way.
The question focuses on functional requirements without surfacing the emotional or social job that is actually driving the decision.
reframing_move: Shift from solution-space to problem-space: instead of 'how do we improve X?', ask 'what progress is the person actually trying to make, and is X even the right thing to improve?' — the quarter-inch-hole reframe forces the question back to the job being hired for.
curation_note: Jobs-to-be-done is one of the strongest reframing models in the catalog because its entire function is questioning the question's framing. The drill/hole metaphor is a canonical example of question-level reframing. The source is explicit: 'the real job a product performs may be significantly different from what the creators initially assume.'

reframing_when.note: All four activations grounded: drill vs hole (Levitt/Christensen), means vs ends (strategic positioning example), user framing mismatch (empathy-driven research), and functional vs emotional job (superficial job definition anti-pattern).

frame_patterns_challenged.note: Proxy optimization: optimizing the drill when the hole is the goal. Means-end conflation: confusing the solution category with the problem space. Symptom as problem: treating the presenting complaint instead of the underlying job.
